articles.title: ‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.”

The change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas , founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.
“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X .

Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

For Muse users, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September , less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas said any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

What’s new is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.
Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the company had nothing to share.

Amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported , and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May , combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant. It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop , much as people do with Muse.

articles.title: Seattle startup Aarden raises $8M to help landowners navigate the AI and energy building boom
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other developments.

Founded last year, the company says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team said it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more important than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason said in a statement.

The company combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.
Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

The new round brings Aarden’s total funding to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The company has 13 employees and plans to nearly double in size over the next 12 months.

Margason said he launched the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations.

One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses.

“Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” said Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres , which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id , which offers property insights and mapping tools.
Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, said the company is already having an impact.
“We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson said on LinkedIn .

articles.title: Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” said Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” users of each company’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.
The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

New MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.
It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “ long term self-sufficiency ,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature shows business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.
Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage .

articles.title: Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

The department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks. Bomb technicians can steer the robot from nearly a mile away to inspect suspicious devices, open doors and move possible explosives into safe containers, SPD said in a blog post last week .

It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD said a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.
The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”
It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.
Boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash , then brought the robots back two years later.

Back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.
And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”

articles.title: Seattle tech vet and Sounders FC minority owner Chee Chew joins front office to lead AI push
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”

Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry . Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.
A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.
It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.
“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

He recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew said, and asked if they could do it every game.
The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox , was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew said he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.
“It has to be approachable for folks,” he said. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”
The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.
“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he said.

articles.title: Satya Nadella kicks off Microsoft Ignite with an Outlook outage mea culpa: ‘We have work to do’
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.
Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella said the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”

“We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he said. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”
The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

It was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.
From there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here .

articles.title: Op-Ed: It's Time to Reconnect Fremont and Grapple with the Barrier Aurora Avenue Creates
articles.author: Ankur Dhoot
paras: In 2021, SDOT began studying improvements to Aurora Avenue with funding from WSDOT and King County Metro. In 2022 , the Washington State Legislature allocated $50 million for a demonstration project in the Licton Springs section of Aurora Avenue. The state wanted design completed by fall 2023 , and for construction to begin in spring 2024. In other words, the state wanted the city to take action quickly.
The city opted to continue studying the entire corridor instead and, in 2024 , the intent to fund $50 million for Aurora was dropped from the state budget.

In the five years since the study began, not much has changed. The most meaningful near-term improvement is likely a signalized crossing of Aurora and N 137th St. Otherwise , a few turn restrictions, hardened centerlines, and repainted crosswalks are all SDOT has to show for five years of work.

The proposed alternatives in the long term corridor study leave much to be desired . The agency's current estimate for when the study will be completed and construction on larger capital projects will begin is now 2031 - a full decade after the study began. (Of course, this assumes funding will be available then.)

We need to build momentum for change along Aurora. Trust is lost when planning and studies take a decade without meaningful near-term changes. Reconnect Fremont is a demonstration project to overcome the existing inertia, rebuild trust with the community, and make people reimagine Aurora as more than a highway bisecting their neighborhood.

Aurora Avenue is classified as an Urban Village Main through Fremont. According to SDOT’s Streets Illustrated guidelines: “ while Urban Village Main Streets must accommodate the movement of people and goods through the Urban Center or Village, the design of these streets encourages slower speeds and clearly communicates that walking, bicycling and transit access are prioritized.”

If you’ve ever traveled along this section of Aurora, you know that walking, bicycling, and transit access are not prioritized. A concrete barrier runs down the center, and there are no street level crossings. For vehicles, this section of Aurora is an uninterrupted freeway. For everybody else, it’s a physical barrier.

Different stretches along Aurora have different problems. The most obvious issue in the Fremont stretch currently is high speeds (speed limits were reduced in other sections of Aurora in 2021, but not in Fremont), no accessible crossings, and a dearth of E Line stops. From N 68th Street near Green Lake to the Aurora tunnel, there is not a single street level crossing.

The E Line is the highest ridership bus line in Washington State. But the only E Line stop in Fremont is at N 46th Street. The nearest northbound stop is at N 65th St, more than a mile away. The nearest southbound stop is at Lynn Street, more than 1.5 miles away. There is only a single E Line stop in a 2.5-mile stretch through one of the densest neighborhoods in North Seattle!

It doesn’t have to be this way. Reconnect Fremont proposes a series of concrete improvements that will restore east-west connectivity, improve transit access, and build momentum for the entire Aurora corridor through near-term action.

As the densest part of Fremont, the desire for an E Line stop at N 38th Street is over a decade old . King County Metro would like to build a stop here, provided that the city and state install a safe street level crossing.

The current walk from the sole E Line stop at N 46th Street to the Fremont core is 20+ minutes . An E Line stop and street level crossing at N 38th Street will provide improved access to the Lower Fremont commercial district, as well as the increasing density along Stone Way.

There is currently a pedestrian overpass at Aurora and N 41st Street, just a block from the B.F. Day Elementary School. In 2025, SDOT completed a seismic retrofit of this bridge at a cost of more than $2 million , despite the schools in the area having previously requested a street level crossing be installed at this location.

The enrollment area of B.F. Elementary School spans both sides of Aurora. Parents with strollers or kids with bikes have an unnecessarily difficult experience trying to cross Aurora using the inaccessible overpass.

As the Seattle School Traffic Safety Committee said , “A safe, pleasant, at-grade crossing will reunite a neighborhood with the happy add-on of making the commercial spaces along Aurora more accessible for all.”

The first neighborhood greenway in Seattle was the Wallingford Neighborhood Greenway (now rebranded a Healthy Street ). It connects to Hamilton International Middle School, Lincoln High School, the Wallingford Playfield, and the Wallingford commercial district along N 45th Street. The Healthy Street currently ends at Stone Way, but there is an opportunity to extend it further west.

The enrollment areas of Hamilton International Middle School and Lincoln High School cross Aurora. The Upper Fremont Neighborhood Center will add density a few blocks west as well, and a 71-unit supportive housing facility already exists on the west side of Aurora and N Motor Place.

A street level, signalized crossing of N Motor Place can extend Seattle’s first Neighborhood Greenway, provide a safe bike connection for kids getting to school, and connect the increasing density in Upper Fremont with the existing commercial district in Wallingford.

The lone E Line stop in Fremont is at N 46th Street and serves more than a thousand riders per day. It is also a transfer point to Route 44 which connects to U District and Ballard. The bus stop is surrounded by on- and off-ramps and high speed traffic.

It is a common sight to see someone hop the jersey barrier to catch the E Line on the other side of Aurora Avenue. A street level, signalized crossing at N 46th Street would provide safe and convenient access to this bus stop.

In 2023, Chief Seattle Club opened the Goldfinch building at Aurora and N 48th Street. In 2026, DESC opened Clover Place at Aurora and N 49th. Plans are currently underway for a multi-purpose athletic field at Woodland Park near Aurora and N 50th Street to serve Lincoln High School. The Woodland Park Zoo (which draws over a million visitors per year) is a few blocks from Aurora and N 50th.

There is significant demand for an E Line stop and street level crossing at Aurora and N 50th. The Woodland Park Zoo has expressed support for such improvements, as have the Friends Of Lower Woodland Park and the neighbors in the area.

There is currently no all ages and abilities bike route from the Burke-Gilman Trail in Fremont connecting to Woodland Park and Green Lake. Most people take Stone Way N, which contains a door-zone bike lane going north and no bike facilities at all going south. Stone Way N is an arterial listed on the High Injury Network , although it got some safety improvements in 2026 as a result of advocacy from Ballard Fremont Green Streets.

Woodland Park Avenue was listed on the original 2014 Bicycle Master Plan and the 2024 Seattle Transportation Plan as a neighborhood greenway. Building this greenway would provide a much-needed connection between the Burke-Gilman Trail and Woodland Park. The main challenges are the crossings of the arterials – Bridge Way N , N 46th Street, and Green Lake Way N – but some improvements are already on the way.

In 2016, a Neighborhood Street Fund application was submitted for crossing improvements at N 46th Street and Green Lake Way N, but was not chosen for funding. In 2026, one of the projects selected in the D4 District Project Fund was an enhanced pedestrian crossing of Bridge Way N at the Woodland Park Avenue intersection.

With the aforementioned signalized crossing of Aurora Avenue and N Motor Place, we can build the desired bike route between the Burke-Gilman Trail and Woodland Park without having to wait for future improvements at N 46th Street and Green Lake Way N. How? In 2022, the Route 44 TPMC built a crossing of Linden Ave N and N 46th . By making a greenway on Linden Avenue N at N Motor Place, we have the connection to Woodland Park. Linden Avenue N is already a proposed greenway in the Seattle Transportation Plan, and this connection would also create a safe route to the Upper Fremont Neighborhood Center .

The Aurora Reimagined Coalition has hosted two walks for Reconnect Fremont . Reconnect Fremont has been presented to the Fremont Neighborhood Council, Seattle School Traffic Safety Committee, Seattle Pedestrian Advisory Board, and Lincoln High School PTSA, and is endorsed by a broad coalition of organizations, such as the Cascade Bicycle Club, Amalgamated Transit Union 587, Ballard Fremont Green Streets, the Downtown Emergency Service Center, the Fremont Chamber of Commerce, the Fremont Neighborhood Council, the Transit Rider’s Union Bus and Transit Service Committee, and Transportation Choices Coalition.
Reconnect Fremont has also received letters of support from Cascade Bicycle Club , Friends of Lower Woodland Park , and the Woodland Park Zoo , and has strong support from state lawmakers.
Let our leaders and decision makers know that you want to Reconnect Fremont - sign the Action Network campaign !

articles.title: Old timers say goodbye to Mediterranean Express as Garlic Crush set to close on Broadway
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Mediterranean Kitchen Express, Mediterranean Express, Garlic Crush — However you knew it, the affordable falafel and shawarma joint has been part of its stretch of Broadway since the 90s.
Thursday will be the restaurant’s final day :

To our amazing Seattle guests, thank you. Thank you for every visit, every shared meal, every kind word, and every memory we’ve made together. Being part of the Capitol Hill community has meant so much to us, and we will truly miss seeing your familiar faces!
You can still visit its sibling locations in Bellevue, Issaquah, Redmond, Woodinville, and, soon, Kirkland, ownership says.

The closure ends a long history of Lebanese flavors on the block. Long run as Mediterranean Express, Maher “Matt” Jabbour took over his brother’s joint in 2019 to make it part of his growing Garlic Crush chain. Not a lot changed and the favorites including excellent garlic fries continued on even as big chain neighbors like Chipotle moved in next door.

The closure comes as the Harvard Market shopping center changed hands earlier this year. CHS reported here as the two-level center and parking facility at Broadway and Pike has been acquired for $14.2 million by San Diego-based developer Tourmaline Capital .
Thanks Google Maps for a few images through the years

While other closures have left blank spots in the center’s street-level mix including the 2024 closure of the block’s AT&T store, improvements and increase security under the new ownership has helped reduce disorder and public safety concerns around the QFC -anchored shopping center.
Meanwhile, some long-term food and drink tenants at Harvard Square have continued to thrive. Ooink is celebrating ten years of craft ramen above Pike and Broadway this year.
As for the Garlic Crush space, a check of city paperwork didn’t reveal any immediate plans for the soon to be emptied restaurant space.
Garlic Crush is located at 1417 Broadway and is planning its final day of business on Thursday, November 19th. Learn more at garliccrush.com .

articles.title: King County’s 2027 budget includes plans for a new $4M tiny house village in the Central District
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: King County and the Low-Income Housing Institute are moving forward with plans to open an 80-unit tiny house village in the Central District in early 2027, part of a broader push to expand shelter capacity for both families and individuals living unsheltered.

According to King County Executive Girmay Zahilay’s office, the county is committing $5 million toward the Spruce Street Tiny House Village as part of a larger supplemental budget package aimed at advancing his goal of creating 500 new housing and shelter units within 500 days. While Zahilay announced a $5 million commitment in September, King County Council budget documents for the proposal specify a $4 million appropriation toward the project’s development as the council reviews the 2026–2027 budget proposal ahead of a final vote scheduled for November 24.

The new village will be situated on county-owned land at the vacant southeast corner of the Judge Patricia H. Clark Children and Family Justice Center campus. LIHI, the nonprofit housing developer and shelter operator that manages 18 tiny house villages across the region, will partner with the county to build and operate the site.

This summer, CHS reported on the opening of LIHI’s Belmont Village , a $1.1 million project that created 31 shelter homes on a Capitol Hill lot eventually destined to be built up to a new 120-unit permanent supportive housing facility from the the Downtown Emergency Service Center .

The county investment comes as Mayor Katie Wilson has also made tiny house villages a centerpiece of hoped-for shelter expansion in the city. This spring, the Seattle City Council approved Wilson’s plan for “Shelter Acceleration” that raised legal limits on residents at “transitional encampments” to 150. The bill also allows one “interim use” 250-resident village in the city. The plan has produced only limited progress including 75 new units at a new village in Interbay. Wilson has slowed her shelter goals under 2027 budget planning . In March, the administration framed the delivery of 1,000 shelter units as a single-year objective for 2026. Wilson is now extending that goal through the end of 2027, scheduling 960 total beds to serve an estimated 1,750 people annually across facilities established in 2026 and eight sites slated for 2027.

The county is leading the way on the Spring Street Tiny House Village funding as it puts its surplus property to use. Just south of Capitol Hill, the county’s $242 million youth jail and justice center opened in the winter of 2020 with 16-cell living halls designed to look like dorms but secured for incarceration with electronic locks and state of the art surveillance systems, new classrooms, and an expanded visitation areas where youth offenders can meet with family and lawyers.

The new tiny village will fill an empty corner on the south of the campus. The area south of the justice center is an ongoing public safety issue for the city where the Wilson administration and the Seattle Police Department have instituted a new approach to street disorder that hasn’t really made a dent in issues at the corner. The blocks in between are happier places including Bailey Gatzert Elementary School and the Washington Hall community venue.

The Central District area has hosted several tiny house villages providing transitional shelter for unhoused residents. Currently, three villages operate in the neighborhood — True Hope Village with 33 units on E Yesler Way, a Low-Income Housing Institute site opened in 2018 on church property for families, couples, and single adults, T.C. Spirit Village with 24 units on 22nd Ave, a LIHI-managed site opened in 2020 at Christ Spirit Church focused on serving Native American, Alaska Native, and Black residents, and Nickelsville Central District on 21st, a resident-governed encampment serving singles, couples, and families.

The neighborhood was home to Seattle’s first officially sanctioned tiny house village that opened in late 2015 on 22nd Ave in partnership with the Lutheran Church of the Good Shepherd before being cleared to make way for Good Shepherd House , an 86-unit permanent supportive housing building that opened in 2024.

Designed as an enhanced shelter rather than a basic encampment, the Spruce Street facility will feature 80 insulated, heated, and lockable tiny houses. According to project plans released by the executive’s office, approximately 30 units will be dedicated to families with children, while the remaining 50 units will serve singles and couples.

Alongside residential units, the site will include a community kitchen, shared gathering space, a children’s play area, hygiene and laundry buildings, and dedicated offices for on-site staff and case managers.

LIHI says that its tiny house village model is intended to serve as a safe, dignified bridge between street homelessness and permanent housing. At existing LIHI villages, on-site case managers assist residents with employment, health services, and housing navigation, helping more than half of exiting households transition into permanent homes in 2025, according to the organization.

Representatives from King County and LIHI have already begun community outreach, presenting site plans to Central District residents at a Squire Park Community Council meeting in October. Pending final budget approval from the King County Council , construction and site preparation are slated to move forward ahead of an anticipated opening in early 2027.

articles.title: The Real Happy Meals Are in Chinatown
articles.author: Michael Wong
paras: People are pissed off at the idea of a McDonald’s posting up in Chinatown . Rightfully so, considering expensive, soulless fast-food restaurants can get mogged any day of the week by any spot on the block. So instead, here are five spots in the CID that would run Ronald McDonald outta town.

Gan Bei If you know anyone who hangs out in the CID, Gan Bei is likely one of their shortlisted go-tos. Since opening in 2018, this quaint spot has been the favorite among restaurant-industry folks who need a cool place to unwind. Upon entering Gan Bei, on Weller St. between 6th and 7th Ave., the bar setup beckons you in; past that, you’ll find places to sit and stay awhile. If you go to McDonald’s for something easy to get and easy to understand, Gan Bei is just the same—a familiar haunt that’s also serving familiar favorites. In a restaurant climate where prices mean consumers may have to share or order less, Gan Bei’s for-the-people way of things is a welcome contrast. For your money, you’re gonna get hit-the-spot Chinese-American food (including claypot items) at great prices with a drink menu that’ll keep you ordering more. Try the roasted garlic smelts as a bar snack ($15) or their chicken with house-made gravy ($14), both sure to show you what a real Happy Meal could taste like.

Oasis Tea Zone Situated in the heart of the CID on 6th Ave. and Weller St, the mecca and mainstay for late-night meetups in the CID is Oasis Tea Zone. Basically, if Oasis is closed, it’s time to go home. Open til midnight most days and til 2 a.m. on the weekends, Asians and folks in the know have frequented this Oasis location for over two decades, with a drink menu that accommodates all boba cravings (more customization, fewer cutesy preset options) and enough seating to never worry about rubbing shoulders with an opp. Where McDonald’s offers a chill place to eat fried foods and scroll on your phone, Oasis provides the same, while also being a perfect place to meet up with friends, clients, dates, attorneys, or the like. Additionally, ball knowers will order their Taiwanese popcorn chicken, which has long been one of the best values in CID, and is available later than you’d expect.

Uwajimaya Deli (After 5 p.m.) One of the most slept-on meal deals in the CID might be Uwajimaya’s hot food counter. Behind the glass, a team member is ready to fill a box with whatever you can point at. Beyond the expected Chinese-fast-food options, Uwajimaya has a rotating cast of banger options like kimchi fried rice, pork adobo, beef chow fun, and of course their Chinese BBQ selection. At daytime price, filling this box will cost you about $15, but after 5 p.m., most locations drop the box price to $10, which is a deal not even fast food can beat. At first you’ll just want to build full meals, maybe for yourself or loved ones. But soon, once you come to better understand the offerings and your palate, you’ll start filling boxes in bulk with one or two of your favorite items, and make rice at home. And beyond the deli-box deal, their BBQ rice combos at regular price are hard to beat, too, if you’re already there. Whether you’re meal prepping or munchie prepping, this is the deal to pin.

Dim Sum King Quick and easy is the McDonald’s way, and the same goes for many Chinese restaurants. So if you’re looking for something you can truly grab on the go, something just as modular as a McValue Menu, there’s no better option in the CID than Dim Sum King. If you can point at it, you can order it, but if you know what you’re doing, grab a pencil and fill out the sheet. Two aunties behind the counter will be fielding orders, both from the slips and from the requests coming in from Cantonese-speaking customers. The tried-and-true dim sum options are all available: shrimp dumplings (har gow), shrimp and pork dumplings (siu mai), and yes, chicken feet too. All available by the piece (starting at $1.20 per), and endlessly composable from there. Given the prices and the speed, it’s easy to over order too, so pace yourself or find some friends. Keep in mind that, a lot like McDonalds, sauce costs extra if you’re planning to eat on the move. And don’t sleep on the mango pudding in the fridge before you go. Thank me later.

Hello Em Việt Coffee & Roaster y I won’t shut the fuck up about Hello Em, or the restaurant empire of Yenvy Pham and her sister Quynh-vy (who together just released a cookbook ). And while any of their spots could and do mog McDonalds already, it’s Hello Em Cafe that I think should put fear in the Golden Arches. First off, the coffee beans come direct from a farm in Buôn Ma Thuột and are roasted in-house. Fair warning, consult your doctor before enjoying multiple coffee beverages from Hello Em, because the stuff works. The menu is inspired, not just coffee cold or hot, so you’ll find a drink that suits the day you want to have, or are currently having. I tend to go for cà phê chuối (Vietnamese coffee with caramelized banana, coconut, pandan egg whip, salted peanuts, and banana chips) or a cà phê with Maggi caramel condensed milk (yes, like that Maggi). Beyond the drinks, what really brings me back is their food, including my favorite pressed pâté breakfast croissant (with fried shallot omelette, bone marrow pâte, and Viet mayo)the perfect 18 bites available at a cafe. Some other delights include their đậu hũ (tofu marinated in pickling liquid with bone marrow pâte, and viet mayo for $8.50) and their xúc xích “việt dog” (polish dog, Viet mayo, hot mustard, and mothafucking Laughing Cow cheese). I’m loving it.

articles.title: The Male Gays
articles.author: Dan Savage
paras: I can’t find a clear answer to this online, Dan, but maybe you can help. Gay man here in an open relationship. If I’m having sex with new partners and taking DoxyPEP afterwards, how long do I have to wait after taking the DoxyPEP before having sex with my primary partner again? Is there a window of time in which I could pass something on to my partner before the DoxyPEP fights it off? If I need to wait until the DoxyPEP takes effect, how long would that wait have to be?

I shared your question with Dr. Peter Shalit, a primary care physician in Seattle and a professor of medicine at the University of Washington. Dr. Shalit has been at the forefront of the gay men’s sexual health movement for decades. He wanted me to make clear that his answer was about DoxyPEP generally, OCD, and not medical advice for you in particular, although Dr. Shalit does use the details you shared as a hypothetical jumping-off point.

“DoxyPEP prevents an infection from getting established,” said Dr. Shalit, “so no wait is needed if it works. So, if OCD has outside sex and then takes DoxyPEP and it works, he can immediately have sex with his primary partner. But OCD needs to bear in mind that DoxyPEP is not 100% effective. It reduces the chance of chlamydia and syphilis by about 70%, and of gonorrhea by somewhat less than 50%. Which means he can still get — and he can still transmit — any of these infections despite using DoxyPEP faithfully.”

So, while you can have sex with your primary partner immediately after fucking someone else and taking your DoxyPEP, OCD, it’s not without risk. If the other person has a sexually transmitted infection and the DoxyPEP doesn’t work — if the med fails to prevent an infection from getting established — you could wind up passing an STI on to your partner.

“If OCD has additional partners but his primary partner does not, his primary partner should consider taking DoxyPEP after each sexual encounter with OCD,” said Dr. Shalit, “and they should both be screened for STIs at regular intervals. If they both have outside partners, then ideally, they should both take DoxyPEP after every sexual encounter — with each other as well as other people.”

I’m a 50-something Gen X gay guy — out and proud since age 24 — writing a memoir about midlife reinvention. Yet here I am, feeling like I’m back in the shadows of the closet, panicking over my own laptop screen. My family thinks I’m writing Eat, Pray, Love when I’m actually writing Eat, Pray, Grindr . It features tastefully explicit sex, the unraveling of an open relationship of almost twenty years, and one atomic secret: I cheated on my ex-husband before we ever opened things up. We divorced twelve years ago, but we’re still close and share the same social circle. He knows I’m writing a book, but he has no idea what’s inside. Two questions:
1. The Family: How do I warn my loved ones about the sex scenes without dying of cringe? Is saying “Skip Chapters 4 and 9 if you don’t want to picture my dick” the appropriate thing to do?
2. The Ex: Do I confess the old affair to him before he reads the manuscript? Or do I let him discover it along with everyone else? How do I own my truth without blowing up my post-divorce peace?

I shared your questions with Sarah Hepola , a 50-something Gen X straight gal. In addition to being Gen X, Hepola the author of the New York Times -bestselling memoir Blackout . Her newest book — The Only Thing There Is to Want — is a very revealing memoir about the three great loves of her life: a married man (!), a much younger man (!!), and a cop (!!!). So, Hepola recently faced the very dilemma you face now.

1. “My childhood hero Stephen King has a great book called On Writing that’s half memoir, half instructional manual. Let me paraphrase him, though he’s probably paraphrasing someone else: Write with the door closed, edit with the door open. So, get this complicated story on the page and don’t worry about the nonsense that makes writers crazy. (What will my family think? what will I wear to the awards ceremony?) What TORID is doing right now is a private matter between him and the page. Most people who start a book will never finish it, but if he does, other questions will emerge: Should he publish? If so, how? (It’s a tough industry!) A book can take anywhere from a year to, in my case, eight years (!) to move through the pipeline, so worrying about what your family will think when they read it is like picking out the drapes for your new house before the thing is even built.”

2. “Once the question of publication looms, TORID faces a different and intriguing question: Is this book meant for a mass audience or was writing it a soft form of confession actually intended for the very people he’s terrified might read it? In other words, maybe the book becomes a published book — again, it’s a gauntlet — or maybe it becomes the story of his life that he wrote in order to share with the people closest to him because he wants them to know he’s not the Gay Elizabeth Gilbert. He’s more the Secret Gore Vidal or something. I don’t know! He may not know either! Bottom line: Get it written, because writing a memoir is fantastic therapy, a brilliant way to reflect on your own role in whatever messes you’ve gotten yourself into, but publishing a memoir is a whole other ballgame . A lot of stories that I write thinking, ‘ Oh man, what will so-and-so say, ’ never get published and then it’s a moot point! However, once the book is actually going to come out, I let people in my life read pages, because that’s how I sleep at night (no bombshells dropped on loved ones), and I think the work gets better and richer and more fully dimensional when the author hears alternate perspectives. That’s just me, though. Others take the ‘forgiveness, not permission’ route, bless their hearts.”

P.S. I’ve written two memoirs — one about becoming a dad, one about getting married — and both included details about my sex life that I didn’t want my mom to read. “There are things a mother has a right not to know,” my mom always said, so I knew she wouldn’t want to read about, say, my first visit to a sex dungeon in Berlin. So, while I sent her huge chunks of both of my memoirs before publication, I didn’t send her everything . And when the books came out, I let her know which chapters to skip.

P.P.S. Allowing your ex to get blindsided by someone who read your book before he had a chance to read it himself — assuming your book gets published at all (it’s a gauntlet, like Sarah said) — would be unforgivably inconsiderate. If you truly value the relationship you have with your ex, TORID, you’ll give him a copy of the book to read in advance and a chance to talk about it with you — privately — before the book is released.
Follow Sarah Hepola on Instagram @thesarahhepolaexperience .

I’m a married gay man in my early 40s living in a very gay city on the West Coast. I am very sex-positive and, while I am not myself kinky, I consider myself kink positive. Here’s what I’m having trouble with: the pups. They’ve been around for a long time, but it seems like there are more and more of them in gay spaces. I was at a pride parade last year with a friend in his pup gear and I couldn’t help but notice that he had the same reaction to actual canines as he would other pups he would see on the street. He would go up to them and howl, bark, pant… both the human pups and the canines. We then came back to our house, my dog started licking him and he was practically gooning over it. I became so uncomfortable that I had to put my dog inside. It just seems to flirt with bestiality too much for my own comfort, and I get extremely uncomfortable around pups in the bars. So, am I just an old-fashioned fag now? Do I need to get over my own discomfort here and get with the times?

articles.title: Immigration enforcement continues to impact local families
articles.author: Jaelynn Grisso
paras: Six-year-old Victoria went to downtown Seattle earlier this year after being called in for an immigration court hearing. Officials had marked her as an “unaccompanied minor” - despite the fact she came to the U.S. with her parents - and separated her case from her parents’ case.
Advocates working closely with families told Cascade PBS they frequently see this process of separating kids' cases from their parents and believe it’s a tactic to sow confusion.

“In the last year we've really seen an escalation in the attacks by ICE on migrant families, migrant children, migrant women," said Anna Beyette, an organizer with International Women’s Alliance. “What we've actually seen, since the start of the year, is the escalation of particularly children's courts into something that they're referring to as ‘mega master’ hearings.”

Those hearings often saw dockets with a hundred cases or more per day. Beyette says the mega master hearings have slowed since this summer, but the number of cases in a regular court day has still gone up. She estimates that dockets had about a dozen cases a day before the mega master hearings began, and now they have an average of 50 60 cases in a regular court day.

In the first half of this year, more than 300 children were arrested as part of immigration enforcement in Washington. But that is only a fraction of the kids who have ongoing cases and could be called into court. Beyette estimates the number of children with hearings this year to be over a thousand.

“It's terrifying for the children. Many of them are young,” Beyette said. “When you go in there, you see families with babies and toddlers who are there for their toddlers' appointments. And so to ask children to advocate for themselves oftentimes in like not their native language, without proper information to them about what's happening, is just really a violation of their human rights.”
Many of those arrested are between 10 and 14 years old. But some arrests are for kids much younger, including a handful that were under a year old.

As for 6-year-old Victoria, Beyette and many others successfully rallied to push for her case to be reconnected to her mom’s case. She says she sees that as a win not just for Victoria, but for every family encountering this situation.

“One thing that I really want to make very clear is that even as there are these heightened attacks on migrant families and our communities, we're seeing people fighting back,” she said. “Even as they're afraid for their families, they're fighting back because migrants always are at the forefront of fighting not just for their families, but to end a system that is forcing them from their homelands and then targeting them when they come here to the U.S.”
Home Depot parking lots were once a place for those looking for a day’s work to gather.
During late summer and early fall, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were responsible for a surge in arrests of day laborers at Seattle-area home improvement big box stores.
In the months since, those crackdowns have reportedly decreased in the Seattle area.
KUOW reporter Gustavo Sagrero Álvarez has been covering immigration enforcement surges at Seattle metro-area Home Depots.

Sagrero Álvarez said what's often not talked about is that the men searching for work span the spectrum of immigration status, including U.S. citizens, asylum seekers, and likely a significant number without legal status.

“One of the gentlemen that I spoke to in the story, he had been here [in Washington] for two years recently, and his family was back in Mexico, and he was here living in the United States - working in the United States without documentation,” said Gustavo Sagrero Álvarez, who covers the intersection of race and identity.

“And he was trying to figure out how to maintain his life here, sustain himself, while also sending what he could back to his family. There are other people, though, that have been here for so much longer. Decades, you know, sometimes even longer than I've been alive. Which is kind of crazy to think, you know, at least for somebody who's 30 years old, right? And these gentlemen have been making a living doing this kind of workday, in and day out for, for that long,” Sagrero Álvarez said.

Since those surges, people looking for work in those parking lots, are often few and far between in the Seattle metro area. However, east of Seattle in Central Washington, Sagrero Alvarez noted similar surges are happening in Yakima, an area with a large Latino population.

The Department of Homeland Security said it has no plans to stop deportations. The agency said in a statement: “ICE is NOT backing away or slowing down. Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation’s laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets.”
Meanwhile, Sagrero Álvarez says many of the men arrested by ICE agents are in varying situations.

“Some folks are still fighting their cases to stay in the United States. articles.title: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands
articles.author: Mark Olalde
paras: A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies.

“Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them.

Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth.

ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules.

Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers.
Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land.

“These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act , which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act , which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives.

“I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress.

Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority.
“These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.”

Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities.

Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes.

The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants , which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued.

Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate.

Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.”
The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land.

articles.title: A heretical outrage: why Italians disown spaghetti bolognese
articles.author: Luca Cesari
paras: Spag bol carries my city’s name all over the world – to the embarrassment of restaurants in Bologna

In Bologna, spaghetti bolognese does not exist. You’ll find it on menus in London and Sydney, in British school canteens and in jars on supermarket shelves across half the world, but not in the city that lent it its name. Order it in a trattoria beneath the Two Towers and at best you get a pitying smile. More often you’ll be brought a plate of tagliatelle, with a short lesson in local history on the side.

Few of the Italian dishes famous abroad carry the name of a city. Every so often the argument flares up again over where pizza, carbonara or tiramisu were born. With spaghetti bolognese the parentage is written into the name, and yet, absurdly, it is the Bolognese themselves who disown it. Many regard it as an outrage, a heretical and misshapen version cooked only by people who know nothing of real Bolognese food.

articles.title: While the term ‘Friendsgiving’ is new, the tradition has been around for decades – found family and experimental freedom make this holiday special
articles.author:
<name>Kirsten Chervenak, Research Associate for the Center for Regional Agriculture, Food, and Transformation, Chatham University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/kirsten-chervenak-2778207"/>
paras: One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.
While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.
If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering.

Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era , when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved.

In her book “ Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality ,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event.

Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity.

Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
What’s your apocalypse skill? Finding a future‑proof hobby can bring fulfilment today
Five ways to enjoy fashion as a hobby without indulging in overconsumption
The ick: The psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you
Today, Thanksgiving is typically viewed as a family holiday.
For some, this may be the gathering that provides the warm, fuzzy holiday feeling many search for. But for others, family holidays are stressful.
A 2023 survey of 2,061 adults found that 9 in 10 people reported experiencing stress around money, lost loved ones, familial conflict or other expectations during the holidays.
As Friendsgiving isn’t an established holiday, participation is difficult to capture. But of 1,000 people surveyed in 2024, 20% said they planned to celebrate Friendsgiving .
A Friendsgiving is the opposite of established kin-keeping traditions. It gives the opportunity to gather with found family , and while the reason for gathering is established, the form is malleable.

Many people choose a potluck-style as a way of sharing the burden for what can be a labor-intensive meal. Others choose to do away entirely with what is considered the “traditional” meal and showcase foods from their own culture or a cuisine they enjoy.

As a parody of a holiday, Friendsgiving gives participants permission to make the holiday their own and be as playful as they wish. So, if I burn my miso butter corn casserole, no one will be disappointed, because they’ve never tasted it before anyway.
While playing with form and bucking traditional structure can be rewarding, there are some things you may want to keep in mind to have a successful Friendsgiving.

In her book “ The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why it Matters ,” author Priya Parker advises anyone planning a gathering to be specific about purpose. This will help decide the form of the event and whom to invite.

Is this a casual gathering with friends? Is fellowship or food more important? Are you hoping to try a recipe your family would never approve? Be specific about your own expectations before you start planning.

The Emily Post Institute, which promotes etiquette and offers resources for a variety of social situations, recommends being flexible with the menu. This is especially important for a potluck-style gathering. As a host, you may want to assign dishes to guests to ensure a balanced meal without eight desserts. If you have the gumption, however, you can throw caution to the wind and see what happens.
It is also important to keep dietary restrictions in mind to make sure everyone feels included and has something to eat.
Make a plan for heating or reheating. The oven is prime real estate during Thanksgiving. You may want to tell guests to bring their dish already cooked to avoid playing oven Tetris.
Finally, tell guests to bring Tupperware. There will be leftovers, and I have found that nothing is better than creating a second plate to take home and heat up the next day.
Alice P. Julier, a professor of food studies at Chatham University, assisted with the writing of this article.
Kirsten Chervenak is a past student of Alice Julier

articles.title: Jensen Huang scandal illustrates why human nature is cybersecurity’s weakest link
articles.author:
<name>Vanessa Bohns, Braunstein Family Professor and Chair of Organizational Behavior, Cornell University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/vanessa-bohns-875380"/>
paras: The end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature.

Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China . The company says no secrets were leaked .

In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “ human factor is truly security’s weakest link .”

Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information.
These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment?

Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks.

Mitnick has been called “ the most notorious hacker of all time .” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets.
He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him.
In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice.

Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email.

Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad , participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email.
When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws , a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have.
Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior , acquiescence and risk-taking .

In a famous 1984 study , a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study , female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change.
The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets.

Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study , participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder.

Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment , illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about.

In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far.

Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings , my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face.

In one study , participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study , in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call.

Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against.
