articles.title: Fighting in Yemen has made crossing the Bab el-Mandeb even more dangerous – jeopardizing aid and refuge for millions
articles.author:
<name>Lauren Carruth, Associate Professor of International Service, American University School of International Service</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/lauren-carruth-312519"/>
paras: In recent days, Iran-backed Houthi forces have gained greater control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital hub of trade, travel and migration between the Middle East and Africa.

The partial closing of the Strait of Hormuz as part of the war in Iran – and escalating conflicts in Yemen , Ethiopia and Eritrea – had already brought this narrow waterway into new global prominence. Control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains critical to military operations and commodity markets throughout the region.
However, the Bab el-Mandeb’s strategic geopolitical and commercial shipping importance has largely overshadowed its role as a critical humanitarian corridor.

Bab el-Mandeb means “gate of lamentation” or, more poetically, “gate of tears” in Arabic. It remains one of the most dangerous migration passages in the world. Last year, more than 900 people died or went missing trying to cross. In October 2026, a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people, many of whom were escaping violence and persecution.
Meanwhile, millions of people in Yemen and throughout the Horn of Africa face destitution or death without access to lifesaving deliveries of humanitarian relief supplies shipped through the strait.

Our years of research and forthcoming book “ Refugees Without Refuge ” demonstrate how the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is key to the lives of millions of people throughout the region seeking safety, opportunity and humanitarian assistance. Protecting the safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies.

Located at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, between the arid coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. On a clear day along the wide beaches and mangrove forests on the coast of Djibouti, you can see the sandy hills on the shores of Yemen, only about 20 to 30 miles away. On starry nights, the scattered lights of coastal towns twinkle across the waters.

For centuries, passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has been vital to global trade in salt, spices, coffee, livestock and other goods. Religious pilgrims, travelers, migrants and traders have long used the strait for relatively easy transport between continents.
Today, people crossing the strait are also escaping poverty, war, political persecution, disasters and gender-based violence .
Hot, tired, financially depleted and frequently sick or injured, refugees and migrants traverse the Bab el-Mandeb at all hours.

Most negotiate passage across the strait on derelict boats with “delalas” – facilitators, brokers or smugglers – in the shadows of coast guard and police patrols and outside United Nations and governmental migration controls.

The numbers of people crossing the strait are difficult to estimate. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration recorded 122,258 arrivals to Yemen from the Horn of Africa – even more than had crossed by that time in 2025. Most of these migrants were from Ethiopia, and most traveled without passports or visas.

Since August, displacement and insecurity throughout the region has worsened, making accurate figures for the numbers of people migrating and the numbers of people dying trying to cross impossible to estimate.

Despite the dangers of this crossing, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains an economic lifeline for millions of people living in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland, Somalia and elsewhere who rely on commercial goods imported from the Middle East and Asia. However, the Houthi forces in charge of increasing swaths of southwestern Yemen now control most critical ports and islands in the strait, increasing the risks and costs of transit and trade.

The strait has either been closed or has become a bottleneck, allowing only limited shipping traffic since September 2026 . Many cargo ships have been delayed or rerouted, causing businesses in fragile regional economies to pass higher transport and fuel costs on to their customers.

The economic effects of costly and delayed shipping and trade through the strait has compounded the broader effects of increased violence and displacement throughout the region. In front of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026, Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar expressed “grave concern” about the sudden influx of Yemeni refugees putting a strain on underresourced coastal towns and refugee camps. The United Nations relief agency, UNHCR, is reporting an outbreak of cholera in the Markazi refugee camp, the primary home to thousands of Yemenis who have fled across the strait into northern Djibouti.

On top of that, the potential for a return to civil war in Ethiopia , and the potential involvement of Eritrea in regional conflicts, may increase population displacement and further disrupt economic markets on both sides of the strait.
As each of these conflicts unfolds, additional pressure will likely be put on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It provides the only feasible passage for many people seeking safety and opportunity abroad.

Keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open and safe is also vital for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Like challenges of commercial shipping, the maritime transit of relief supplies , including food and medicine, has been undermined by security risks, shipping delays and the rising costs of food and fuel.

UNICEF’s latest situation report for Somalia , published in August 2026, estimates that nearly 5 million people there are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. At least another 5.5 million people in Ethiopia are also in need , due to the effects of conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño.

In Yemen, an estimated 321,000 people have been displaced since Aug. 1, 2026, and ongoing water scarcity combined with conflict has left 17 million people without access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene services. As casualties mount and cholera spreads, hospitals have struggled to obtain essential supplies.

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of all of these crises. It remains a vital human and humanitarian corridor for millions of people needing refuge and relief. It is a lifeline as much as a geopolitical and economic linchpin.
Ensuring the safe passage of people and supplies of humanitarian relief through these waters is necessary to save lives and protect precarious livelihoods throughout the region.

articles.title: Why Americans are losing confidence in public education
articles.author:
<name>Michael P. Evans, Associate Professor of Family, School & Community Connections, Miami University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/michael-p-evans-1509670"/>
paras: Americans’ satisfaction with public education has fallen to its lowest level since 1999.
Less than a third of Americans were satisfied with public education in 2026, compared with more than half who felt this way in 2019 and 1999, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll .

Parents typically give their own children’s education higher marks, reflecting a broader tendency to view familiar local institutions more favorably. But parents’ satisfaction with their children’s schools has also reached a record low: 66% of parents reported being satisfied in 2026, down from 83% in 1999.

Declining test scores, misinformation about public education , culture war issues and a general lack of knowledge about what K-12 schools are teaching have all contributed to this drop in satisfaction.

As an education researcher focused on family, school and community relationships , I am concerned that declining satisfaction in public schools could have lasting consequences for students and communities.
Public education in the U.S. was shaped by 19th-century advocates who argued that universal, free and nonsectarian education was essential to the success of a democratic society.

Communities agreed to invest in education because they believed it would benefit everyone, not just families with children, by supporting economic growth and preparing people to work together to solve shared problems.
Sustaining that public investment depends in part on people’s confidence that schools are delivering on these shared goals.

Without that public confidence, schools may struggle to secure the necessary funding and buy-in from the community. Parents may start to doubt that their children will be well-educated in public schools.
The rise of political polarization in the U.S. has complicated people’s perceptions of education.

Local schools have become flash points in debates over race, gender and what children should learn, and research on school board meetings shows how these conflicts can fuel distrust of school leaders and disrupt how schools are run .

For example, some conservative politicians , media outlets and advocacy groups have promoted false claims that schools are using critical race theory – meaning the idea that racism is built into laws, rules and everyday systems in society – to indoctrinate children.

Researchers found that these campaigns have often distorted lessons about racism and efforts to support students from diverse backgrounds , despite no evidence that critical race theory was widely taught in K-12 schools.
Repeatedly hearing and reading misinformation about public education can make it harder for communities to distinguish reliable, fact-based information from politicized distortions of reality.
The effects of misinformation can also extend into other areas of school life, including the work that district superintendents and school boards do.

In a 2026 study, my colleagues and I found that 82% of district superintendents felt increasingly concerned about inaccurate information circulating about their schools or district decisions . Another 55% reported that school board meetings had become noticeably more contentious over the past few years.

Disputes over teaching about race and racism, the rights of LGBTQ+ students and access to books cost public schools US$3.2 billion during the 2023-24 school year . This estimate includes legal expenses, security, staff time and the cost of replacing employees who left because of tension or fighting at schools.
Controversy and polarization surrounding public schools can leave teachers feeling that their work is not trusted or valued.
Approximately 47% of teachers believed most Americans trusted teachers little or not at all, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center survey.
Teachers who feel valued are more likely to want to stay in the profession . Feeling undervalued may make an already demanding profession less appealing .
Regaining people’s trust in public education would involve the difficult task of addressing legitimate public concerns, like students’ declining test scores .
It would also involve effectively correcting misinformation and diplomatically managing community members’ diverse values and opinions.
Transparency is not just about giving community members more access to information about what schools are teaching and how.
I believe it also means that schools should acknowledge their limitations , explain their decisions and respond to community members’ questions .

For example, when parents voice concerns about how race and racism are discussed in classrooms, educators could share teaching materials, explain their learning goals and provide opportunities for questions.

This could help clarify what students are actually learning, correct inaccurate ideas and spark discussions about how these topics should be addressed. These conversations may not result in consensus, but participants gain a clearer understanding of school decisions and the differing views within communities.
School administrators could also connect with families and community members to give them a chance to ask questions, share concerns and brainstorm solutions.

The Family Leadership Design Collaborative , for example, is a national network led by academics, families, educators and community leaders from across 10 U.S. cities. It works to identify shared educational concerns and draft responses to big educational challenges, including school discipline and racial inequities.

These types of partnerships require a significant commitment. But they offer a chance to give people firsthand opportunities to see how schools can respond to challenges, and to rebuild trust in communities.

articles.title: Your gut bacteria helps your body keep track of time, and when you eat influences how much nutrition you get from food
articles.author:
<name>Zheng Kuang, Associate Professor of Biological Sciences, Carnegie Mellon University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/zheng-kuang-2774380"/>
paras: How your body processes food is significantly influenced by daily rhythms tied to 24-hour light-dark cycles. In new research published in the scientific journal Cell Host & Microbe, my colleagues and I found that the microbes living in your gut are the hidden timekeepers behind this system.

Gut microbes convert dietary signals into molecules that intestinal cells use to synchronize nutrient absorption with feeding times. In mice, this microbe-controlled timing mechanism maximizes the nutrients the mouse’s body takes in and supports growth, especially when food is scarce.
When mice consumed an excess of calories, however, that same system fueled obesity .

Because of Earth’s rotation, all animals – including humans – experience rhythmic shifts of day and night . Your eyes and brain use light signals to coordinate your body’s activities with environmental changes and nutrient availability. Disruption of this temporal alignment, such as through jet lag and night-shift work, is associated with a range of health disorders .

However, light is not the only timekeeper. Your intestines are home to trillions of microbes, called the gut microbiome . They play a key role in shaping your physiology, such as metabolism, immunity and even brain activity.

Intriguingly, the microbiome also influences the daily biological rhythms of hosts . My colleagues and I had previously shown that depleting gut bacteria in mice weakens circadian rhythms in the small intestine and alters them in the colon . These disruptions can affect how well your intestine absorbs and processes fats and other lipids, which may contribute to metabolic disorders such as obesity.
But if gut microbes are never exposed to the light, how do they track time? New research from my team suggests that the answer is feeding time.

We found that the gut microbiota can metabolize phytate – a food component commonly found in grains, beans, nuts and seeds – and convert it into molecules that activate a specific protein in intestinal cells, subsequently turning on genes involved in transporting nutrients. Conversely, when fasting, a decrease in phytate levels leads to reduced microbial activity and a drop in nutrient absorption.
Through this pathway, microbes align intestinal absorption with when you typically eat , which maximizes the efficiency of nutrient absorption.
Our findings suggest that, like light, food provides time-of-day signals that gut microbes read to determine how your body functions.
People have co-evolved with their gut microbiota for millennia, implying this microbe-controlled time system carries benefits.

For most of human history, food was scarce . We hypothesized that this microbial pathway might help people survive and grow under starvation conditions. To test this idea, we fed mice a nutrient-poor diet and gave some of them either a common gut microbe or a molecule it produces that is linked to circadian regulation. We found that undernourished young mice who were given this bacterium or the microbial molecule grew taller and healthier than mice that weren’t, suggesting that this microbial pathway promotes growth and metabolic health when nutrients are limited.

However, many people today have constant access to abundant calories. Rather than nutrient scarcity, obesity has become the dominant dietary challenge. We found that for mice under high-calorie conditions, this microbial pathway promotes excess fat uptake in the body and worsens diet-induced obesity.

Therefore, the same gut microbiome mechanism that helped people thrive can become a liability when it encounters an environment it was never designed for. This is an example of evolutionary mismatch .
Zheng Kuang receives funding from National Institutes of Health and Shurl and Kay Curci Foundation.

articles.title: ‘Strict liability’: The legal standard that could help rein in AI
articles.author:
<name>Deven Desai, Professor of Business Law and Ethics; Associate Director for Law, Policy, and Ethics at the Machine Learning Center, Georgia Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/deven-desai-1518552"/>
paras: Some people have begun using the legal system to rein in AI companies and the harms they are creating. Cases are mounting.

In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that it’s ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, leading to her death . In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot’s interactions with her son contributed to his suicide . The state of Kentucky later filed suit , claiming that Character.AI’s software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation.
Social media companies, powered by artificial intelligence, are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused.
Regulating AI was a hot issue during the 2026 midterms, too. Several candidates who won their races have a regulation agenda .
I am a former litigator and a professor of business law , and all this action signals to me that people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm.

But what is the legal liability of AI software? An answer may be found in a principle known as strict liability . Applied properly, strict liability could restrain the risky parts of the AI industry and still allow it to provide the tools the public wants.

Tort law protects people from negligence, such as who is responsible if you slip and fall in a store . Strict liability is part of tort law, but it is used to hold a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent or had no intent of creating trouble.

Two types of strict liability matter for AI. One addresses abnormally dangerous activity , such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material. The other addresses when a product hurts someone using it .

AI programs likely fit the abnormally dangerous standard. The touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868. In the decision, the court stated that if someone has “anything” under their power that is “likely to do mischief if it escapes, [he] must keep it in at his peril” and is “answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape.” The defendant is liable even if they used “ the utmost care to prevent the harm .”

An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software that is supposed to stay in a sandbox – a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network – but loses control of it . The AI industry’s recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger. When Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October, numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks that its frontier AI models could pose.

One hitch in applying this type of strict liability is that an activity must not be in common usage . Lawyers could make a strong case against so-called rogue AI that runs wild and isn’t available to most people.

Applying the danger standard could still fail to rein in AI companies or reward victims appropriately. In 1929, aviation was seen as abnormally dangerous . But damages were capped at US$8,300, which was not a large deterrent.

Attitudes changed in 1999, when the Montreal Convention standardized strict liability rules for international flights worldwide. It raised statutory damages and eliminated caps for negligence claims. Perhaps the most powerful tool in aviation liability today is for an authority to ground a company’s aircraft, which happened to Boeing after two fatal crashes with its 737 MAX planes.

Strict product liability is the other strategy for holding AI companies responsible for harm. In years past, courts tended to not see software as a product because it is intangible. But that view is shifting . In recent lawsuits alleging that social media hurt people, courts did see social media as a product and concluded that strict liability was applicable . Cases against Facebook have fallen into this category.

Character.AI’s recent bankruptcy filing came in part because of a lawsuit in which the court treated the software as a product . “ Design defects ” is the part of the doctrine gaining traction. To use this, a plaintiff shows that the product posed a foreseeable risk to someone using it. So far, the doctrine has worked when applied to the lack of guardrails in chatbots.

Pursuing strict liability could still run into snags. A court might order that AI software be turned off, or “grounded,” until it is improved. But as AI software creeps closer to being an operating system and is evermore embedded in everyone’s daily activities, it becomes difficult to suspend its use.

AI software by its nature is constantly “learning” and therefore changing. It is impossible for a company to promise that AI software will absolutely behave a certain way . In many cases, AI software is inherently incapable of supporting a guarantee about design safety. Still, strict liability is a way to hold the maker responsible, “even when those products evolve in ways not specifically desired or foreseeable by their manufacturers ,” according to a Brookings Institution report.

I believe that if people are going to accept AI software as a boon to society, tough rules and sharp deterrents are needed. A strict liability system would shift risk from society to the companies seeking vast revenues.

The next steps will be sorting out whether to treat all or some AI software as a product, and whether the technology is ultrahazardous. If it is treated as that dangerous, AI can develop with incentives to reduce harms and ensure that people injured are compensated.
Deven Desai owns shares in Google, Inc. He received unrestricted research gifts from Google, Inc. and Facebook, Inc. a decade ago. He has not been employed by Google since 2010.

articles.title: Lawmakers Turn to a 'Highway Use Fee' to Bolster Sagging Transportation Budget
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: State legislators who have been trying in vain for years to find a more sustainable funding source to replace Washington's waning gas tax are set to try a new tactic in 2027. House Transportation committee chair Jake Fey (D-27th, Tacoma) is gearing up to introduce a new "highway use fee" to help salvage a state transportation budget that continues to invest more in the expansion of the highway network than in the preservation and and maintenance of existing infrastructure.

Thanks to increased fuel efficiency and some degree of compact urban planning, gasoline usage in Washington is never expected to return to a 2018 highwater mark again, with projections instead predicting a steady decline. Revenue from the state gas tax – currently set at 56.5 cents per gallon – is expected to decline in future years as well, even after a six-cent gas tax increase in 2025 that was paired with a future 2% annual inflation adjustment.

This fall, Rep. Fey has been holding a series of "listening sessions" with different groups around the state involved in transportation planning about the highway use fee, though the proposal has been floating around for some time. Lawmakers are expecting a bill to be filed in the lead up to the 2027 session, which begins January 11.

While some details are still being ironed out – hence the listening sessions – the broad contours of a highway use fee are clear. Drivers renewing their car tabs would be charged an additional fee if the published fuel economy standard of their vehicle falls above a certain level. The more fuel-efficient that vehicle is, the higher the fee. In Virginia, where the existing highway use fee is seen as the model for Washington State, that level is 25 miles per gallon. Only vehicles weighing 10,000 pounds or less are set to be covered, taking freight vehicles out of the equation.

Virginia's fees currently range from around $7 for a 25-mpg vehicle to approximately $75 for some of the most fuel-efficient hybrids. Right now, it's not clear whether or how Washington would adjust existing hybrid and electric vehicle fees, which are currently $225 for all vehicles with an electric range of at least 30 miles.

"I would call a bit of a modernization of our transportation system revenues," Fey said last week in a presentation at the Puget Sound Regional Council, speaking to local elected officials. "We are bound and have been utilizing user fees, whether it's tax on fuel or whether it's fees on vehicles, as our primary revenue source. We do have what one could call a highway use fee in terms of existing electric and hybrid [vehicle] fees, but we do still have a fuel tax revenue gap."

Fey noted he is planning to advance the highway use fee with the support of several other legislators including Rep. Julia Reed (D-36th, Queen Anne), vice chair of the House's transportation committee, and Senator Javier Valdez (D-46th, Northeast Seattle).

Though legislators turned to debt this year to balance the transportation budget, issuing $500 million in bonds to keep the 520 bridge replacement project on track in addition to $800 million for overdue bridge and highway upkeep, the work of transportation budget writers is expected to remain challenging. According to the state's Office of Financial Management, transportation revenues are currently expected to be $599 million lower through 2031 compared to the budget that was approved this past March.

In designing a program that charges drivers more for having fuel-efficient vehicles, Fey's proposal will likely not earn him much acclaim among environmental advocates looking to encourage electric vehicle adoption. But he framed his proposal as helping to make the question of who contributes to maintaining transportation infrastructure more fair.

"We've got people who are generally at the lower economic part of our economy that can't afford a new car, a fuel-efficient car for the most part, they're paying more in gas taxes than someone that can afford to buy a very highly efficient vehicle that would be unaffordable for many people," Fey said. "So this is trying to create a little bit more balance and fairness in terms of who pays into the system."

While likely still a heavy lift during a time of heavy scrutiny on additional taxes, the push for a highway use fee will represent a pivot away from a per-mile user fee that looked to be the primary path toward a long-term gas tax replacement. Concerns had been raised with the privacy impacts of creating a road usage charge on top of cost impacts, but it would have also been a significantly heavier lift for the state to stand up.
Fey said that unlike a per-mile road usage charge, a highway use fee could be in place by late 2028 if it were approved next year.

While more difficult to implement, a road usage charge would be fairer from the perspective of scaling fees to mileage, so drivers who rack up tons of miles on state roads pay their fair share, while people who drive sparingly get rewarded relative to their peers. In comparison, an annual highway use fee is a blunt instrument that does not create an incentive to drive less.

One major element of the behind-the-scenes wrangling to come will be how exactly revenues from a highway use fee get distributed. While the majority of gas tax revenue currently goes to the state transportation budget, slices of those dollars do get handed out to cities and counties dealing with transportation funding struggles of their own. Whether there should be some degree of local pass-through – a familiar discussion to anyone following the transportation funding debate at the King County Council earlier this year – will be hotly debated.

Ultimately, a highway use fee is not likely to generate revenue on par with the gas tax. Virginia's current system generates around $100 million per year, compared to the $1.5 billion per year that is generated by Washington's motor vehicle fuel tax.

But it could act as a stopgap, giving lawmakers another tool as some major highway projects look to be coming down the pike, including the replacement of the westbound US 2 trestle in Everett and I-5 through the Nisqually Delta near Olympia. Of course, if state transportation revenue does continue to largely help to fund big-ticket highway projects at the expense of maintaining state and local transportation infrastructure, the legislature might end up in the exact same spot in just a few years, searching for new revenue tools that will enable them to keep pace.

articles.title: As Annapurna Cafe prepares for a big 2027 — and bigger 2028 — it is saying goodbye to Yeti Bar
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: It’s your final week to enjoy the Yeti Bar .
Annapurna Cafe’s Broadway-level hangout next to the west Capitol Hill Station entrance is shutting down after a short, unsuccessful search for a buyer.

Annapurna’s Roshita Shrestha says the decision came down to costs. The closure of the bar comes as Annapurna continues serving below with a big year ahead preparing for a move to a new Broadway space.

CHS reported here on Shrestha and Sujan Sharma’s preparations for the move into a commercial condominium space they purchased on the north end of Broadway years ago to be ready for the 23-year-old restaurant’s eventual relocation.

Annapurna’s current home has long been lined up for redevelopment as a six-story, 50-unit mixed-use building under plans first approved a decade ago . That project was put on ice due to landmarks protections . Any new development plan will need to incorporate preservation of the building’s historic proportions, look, and feel.
The extra time has allowed Annapurna to stay put at 1833 Broadway and will give the Himalayan joint even more time to manage its move to the bigger, better North Broadway space.

Shrestha said that they are starting the paperwork for the overhaul of the new location this fall but the plan is for Annapurna to make the move north in the spring of 2028, leaving 2027 as a year of preparation and construction. In the meantime, Annapurna will continue serving at 1833 Broadway and might continue operating a lunch and takeout business in the space even after the move depending on how long the old building will remain standing.
Star Sushi can continue its run in the space lined up for Annapurna until the buildout and upgrade work takes place in the coming year.

Yeti Bar is less fortunate. Annapurna first opened the street-level sibling bar in 2015 with hopes of launching a higher margin approach to its flavors of Nepal with cocktails and happy hour bites. It was also a celebration of survival as Annapurna shook off the dust from years of light rail construction on the block.

Like many old Capitol Hill favorites experimenting with new Capitol Hill formats, Yeti Bar provided new energy but didn’t hugely change Annapurna’s business prospects. Still, Shrestha says, after 11 years, the bar has had its regulars who will be sad to see it go. She is planning to preserve some of the art from the space to take along through Annapurna’s changes. The final night at Yeti Bar is slated for Saturday.
After that, the Annapurna family will be looking at the year ahead and counting down the days until the spring of 2028.
Annapurna remains open at 1833 Broadway. Follow @annapurnacafeseattle for updates.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, November 16–22
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: (LITERATURE) Like many millennials, I grew up religiously watching LeVar Burton’s iconic educational PBS TV show Reading Rainbow , and it helped instill a love of reading in me early on. However, it wasn’t until watching the charming 2024 documentary Butterfly in the Sky: The Story of Reading Rainbow that I fully appreciated Burton’s cultural impact. Besides his work as a fierce literacy advocate, Burton also starred as main character Kunta Kinte in the groundbreaking 1977 ABC miniseries Roots and as Geordi La Forge in Star Trek: The Next Generation . He’s now telling his own remarkable story in his memoir Take My Word for It , which details his childhood during the Civil Rights Movement and his path to becoming an actor. Burton will join speaker, host, and cultural producer Kiesha B. Free, founder of the community resource directory Hey, Black Seattle!, for a conversation at Benaroya Hall. ( Benaroya Hall, 7:30 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(FILM) Even as a die-hard Eric Rohmer lover, who believes he’s the second greatest French director of all time (Agnès Varda is obviously first), My Night at Maud’s was initially a hard sell for me. Firstly, because it’s about a Catholic engineer’s struggle with faith (snooze), and secondly, because it’s filmed in black and white, which is uncharacteristic for Rohmer’s typically color-drenched films. Little did I know, this film is far from a snooze, and even further from visually uninteresting. My Night at Maud’s is an unsung Christmas classic that takes place in the days leading up to Midnight Mass. There are glittering lights. There is a decorated tree. There are beautiful French people sulking about the holidays. What more could you ask for? ( SIFF Uptown, 7:30 pm ) AUDREY VANN

(MUSIC) Always All Ages: The Vera Project and Black Lodge are hosting a week of FREE shows and classes to celebrate 25 years of all-ages music, art, and community. Between the big names like AJJ, Deerhoof, Kimya Dawson and comedy by Chris Gethard and Demi Adejuyigbe, Friday and Saturday went quick, as free tickets do. Sometimes all-ages shows make me feel like a weird old guy with his arms crossed, but mostly they make me feel really glad that these resources are available to kids who are cooler than I was at that age anyhow. If you’re just finding out about these shows here in the newspaper, don’t fret, there will be very limited tickets available at the door—not to mention a banging local lineup on Wednesday Nov 18 featuring stand-outs Jackie Tulsa (whose 2026 album Good Year rules). ( Vera Project, 7 pm, free, all ages ) DYLAN BUECHE

(MUSIC) How lucky are we that Julien Baker chose Seattle for her three-night rock club residency tour. Just five cities made the cut: Salt Lake City, UT; Cambridge, MA; Carrboro, NC; Lawrence, KS; and Athens, GA. First the Seahawks win the Bad Bunny Super Bowl and now this? Mayor Katie Wilson’s Seattle really is where dreams come true! Baker may most commonly be known as one-third of boygenius, but she’s an incredible solo talent. Her songs, sometimes laden with sweeping piano and always packed with raw emotions, take hold of your heart and squeeze it until it starts to hurt and you start to squirm, but the squirming is where the healing happens. Judging from previous setlists, she seems to pull from the same pool of songs each night (good to know for anyone hoarding tickets to all three shows hoping for some kind of complete multi-day retrospective), but all Baker eras are there— Sprained Ankle , Turn Out the Lights (aka my depression’s personal soundtrack), and Little Oblivions —as well as yet-to-be-released tracks. Go ahead and skip your antidepressant for the day. Let Dr. Baker heal you. (Neumos, 7 pm, all ages) MEGAN SELING

(VISUAL ART) Tapestries made of AstroTurf and buckskin, blankets woven from ink and tape, a Cree prayer rendered in blood-red acrylic and powdery pastel: One of the year’s most anticipated shows (mine at least) opens this month at the Frye. An Indigenous Present is a traveling exhibition co-organized by the renowned artist Jeffrey Gibson and independent curator Jenelle Porter that includes major works and commissions by 15 Indigenous artists, spanning 100 years of Indigenous art. The exhibition embodies a shift in how Indigenous identity is represented within institutional spaces, as artists move beyond redefining their place within these institutions to actively defying the colonial constraints and expectations they have imposed for centuries. Alongside An Indigenous Present , the museum has mounted My Body Is a Basket , featuring work by three Indigenous Pacific Northwest artists—Brenda Mallory, Danielle Morsette, and Sara Siestreem—who push traditional basket weaving into unexpected conceptual and metaphorical territory. ( Frye Art Museum, 11 am-5 pm ) AMANDA MANITACH
A Musical Tribute to Fallen Hip-Hop Soldiers

(MUSIC) As a part of Diabetes Awareness month, Tisha Gallow, who certainly deserves the title The Queen of South Seattle, is presenting a tribute to rappers who passed away: Biggie Smalls, Phife Dawg, Eazy E, DMX, MCA, Tupac, and more. The show will involve live contributions by some of Seattle’s best players: Roc Phizzle, Rick Pitts, and Ngoma Numu. Vitamin D will be on the ones and twos. And you will be there to say, in the words of the late Guru, “I wish you were still living, in memory of….” Rest In Peace. ( Columbia City Theater, 8 pm, 21+ ) CHARLES MUDEDE

(MUSIC) For my fellow millennials who were raised by Nickelodeon and are activated like a sleeper agent by the words “Move it, football head!”: this one’s for us. Award-winning composer Jim Lang, known for scoring the Hey Arnold! series and its associated films, is bringing the beloved animated show’s music on the road in honor of its 30th anniversary (!), along with series creator Craig Bartlett and the official touring band, the PS 118 All Stars. Indulge in some ’90s nostalgia as you revisit the show’s greatest hits—by the way, did you know the cartoon’s fictional setting Hillwood, Washington is an amalgamation of Seattle, Portland, Brooklyn, and Chicago? That makes this a homecoming of sorts! ( Neptune Theatre, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

articles.title: Slog AM: Officials Say Ground Stop Wasn’t AI’s Fault, Longview Mill Had Problems Before Explosion, Old People Are Buying Teslas
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Ground town: The US airspace completely shut down on Friday, grounding flights nationwide. Delays and cancellations continued throughout the weekend. A communications network failure caused the Federal Aviation Administration to ground flights out of an abundance of caution. Officials blame a new router in Arkansas flooding the system with new information after a system upgrade. This was part of an effort to replace copper wire with fiber optic cable.

It definitely wasn’t the FAA’s new AI, officials say . The $875 million SMART system the FAA just started rolling out to “predict problems in the sky” is not the culprit, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and the startup that designed the system. Pretty odd timing, though, you gotta admit!
Trump has finally spoken out about the ground stop: He has identified a new culprit. It’s Joe Biden, of course:

Microsoft products are functioning again: Hip, hip, hooray! Outlook is back. Microsoft said the outage that rendered several of its most critical products useless for over 24 hours last week was not a cyberattack and it was not related to AI. The outage was “an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” Microsoft told KUOW .

Trump goes to China: He’s meeting China’s leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen. This will be Trump’s first meeting with Xi this year without ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang usually attends these trips and has been central to shaping Trump’s views on the US’s technological competition with China. Trump says he doesn’t intend to bring the Nvidia situation up to Xi, including the allegations that a Chinese spy cavorted with Huang. He’ll leave that conversation up to Xi.
Vladimir Putin will also join this trip: It’ll be the first time Xi, Trump, and Putin have all met up together. Probably only good things can come from that meeting.

Meanwhile, in Huang World: After his resignation last week, new CEO Colette Kress is going to “ rein in ” some of the chipmaker’s deals. Nvidia had been functioning as a blank check for burgeoning AI companies. We’ll see how long that lasts; Huang may be flirting with a comeback as CEO.

Longview mill collapse could’ve been avoided: A new Seattle Times report looks into just how often Nippon Dynawave Packaging put off maintenance in the lead-up to the tank rupture that killed 11 workers earlier this year. Since 2019, the mill had “more than 30 spills, toxic releases, and chemical-related injuries.”

Cool, cool, cool: Israel has utilized the facial recognition platform run by Seattle’s neighborhood bookseller to analyze Palestinians. Israel uploaded 3.5 million pictures of Palestinians to Amazon’s AI-powered facial analysis platform Rekognition. In recent years, Israel has moved tons of data into Amazon’s data centers. This includes “sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation,” reports the Guardian .

Senior moment: Elderly Americans whose faculties have declined enough so they don’t drive themselves anymore are buying Teslas for the self-driving feature . That isn’t how it’s supposed to be used. Tesla’s self-driving feature requires supervision and human intervention if the system makes a mistake. Yet, Tesla isn’t advising against these new users; in fact, Tesla is supporting them and using testimonials from people who should not be behind any wheel as advertising. Car-dependence and lack of autonomy without an automobile is so very American. If only they knew about buses.
ICYMI: SNL got a little too real (compliment) in this sketch. Send it to your mom, aunt, or sister.

articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Drops Design Director
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Michael Eliason, Director of Design & Policy at the Seattle Social Housing Developer (SSHD), departed that role last month in a personnel move that signals a strategic pivot for a public development authority still finding its footing. Eliason's former position will no longer exist, with the SSHD instead planning to hire a Director of Policy with a different portfolio of work.

Seattle voters created the social housing developer in 2023 by initiative, providing a mandate for the production of mixed-income, permanently affordable housing, operating independently of Seattle City Council or mayoral control. Two years later, voters approved a dedicated funding source for social housing via a high-earners payroll tax , with early revenue dramatically exceeding expectations in a way that has given the SSHD significant forward momentum .

Eliason had been brought on in January, after being closely involved in advocacy around Seattle's two social housing initiatives. Prior to becoming staff, he had served as one of the developer's first board members, an appointment made via members of Seattle's Green New Deal Oversight Board. Eliason's influence was credited with mandates for Passivhaus design being incorporated into the developer's mission from the jump.

Passivhaus standards create buildings that are highly energy efficient, using thermal insulation, airtightness, and filtered ventilation. While more expensive at the outset, the design creates cost savings as energy costs are reduced, with a benefit of providing more comfortable interior spaces that are more climate-friendly at the same time.

As a strong evangelist for Passivhaus standards and improved urban design, Eliason has pushed for green building requirements for social housing as a contributor for The Urbanist as well as in a book titled Building for People .

Eliason exited the developer just as it has appeared to hit its stride, announcing its first new construction project in the Central District and its second building acquisition in Delridge in the span of just a few weeks. After the SSHD board replaced its initial pick for CEO, Roberto Jimenez, with Interim CEO Tiffani McCoy – who had led the push for social housing in Seattle as co-founder of the advocacy group House Our Neighbors – things appeared to fall into place.
More social housing projects are expected to be announced soon, with a goal of owning 1,000 units by the end of 2027 and putting more in the construction pipeline.
In a post on LinkedIn made shortly after his departure, Eliason characterized the decision as a pivot away from an emphasis on design in future social housing buildings in Seattle.

"I recently learned that design would no longer be a priority for the Seattle Social Housing Developer, as they eliminated the Director of Design & Policy position," Eliason wrote. "It was an exciting run, and I am proud of the work I accomplished with the nearly three-year effort on the board, and then transitioning to staff. This work included massive efforts around standing up the real estate committee and working on the strategic plan - to finding viable and high quality parcels (not on arterials!), steering procurement efforts with architecture firms, working on legislative and local land use policies to deliver more/better/cost effective housing, and adding new construction values - all of which would go on to inform the design standards for new housing."

But sources familiar with how operations at the developer have disputed his characterization, instead pointing to a shift that has occurred as the SSHD has been navigating rules around public procurement for construction projects. Earlier this year, the SSHD rolled out a roster of design firms that will be considered for future developments, including CAST Architecture, Neiman Taber, Mithun, Schemata Workshop, and Perkins Eastman.

With those firms handling the bulk of design work, the SSHD does have less of a need for in-house design expertise, but did recently bring on Jacqui Aiello, former architectural designer at SMR Architecture, a firm focused on affordable housing. Aiello's hire could cut against the assertion that the developer is de-prioritizing design work.

"The Seattle Social Housing Developer made a sincere effort to keep Michael Eliason on staff by providing him with several options," SSHD Director of Communications Lilly Ana Fowler told The Urbanist. "We wish him the best with future endeavors and sincerely thank him for all his contributions to social housing. SSHD takes design seriously and is working with a number of architecture firms on both small and large social housing projects that prioritize family-sized housing, Passive House standards, open spaces and Universal Design."
Eliason did not respond to a request for comment from The Urbanist for this story.

The new Director of Policy position will be tasked with advocating for legislative changes to make it easier to build social housing in Seattle, and with representing the developer in front of governmental authorities, including the Seattle City Council. Rather than leading the design team, the role will be focused on translating "technical legal and regulatory ideas into clear, compelling information for audiences ranging from elected officials and agency staff to community members, the Board, and the media," according to a job posting from this month.

articles.title: Alternative Transit Modes
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: As I explained in an earlier guideway post, Sound Transit chose light rail technology to make it easier to use the existing transit tunnel and to run and stop at grade but many new technologies have been developed since. As Sound Transit builds a lot more elevated and tunneled sections and opens new lines in urban areas, it may need to reevaluate that decision. Sound Transit and Metro already use buses, heavy rail (for Sounder), ferries, and trams. Other cities like San Francisco, Mexico, and Paris use even more different modes like people movers and gondolas. In that post I talked about monorail and maglev guiderail systems. They are easier and faster to build due to prefabricated guideways, are slicker and therefore visually less obtrusive, and may offer easier maintenance.

As Sound Transit is facing escalating construction costs and feels it cannot accommodate traditional elevated trains downtown, it may be a good time to evaluate these and other alternative transit modes. Monorail systems have opened in Bangkok, and TSB has built a maglev test line in China and is looking at several options in Germany. Swyft Cities (working with Whoosh Solutions) and Ottobahn are working on cabins which hang from a guideway like the Wuppertaler Schwebebahn and provide personal rapid transit (PRT).

Similar to a Waymo or Zoox robotaxi, Swyft Cities and Ottobahn offer more route flexibility, are called via phone app, and have small individual cabins with an electric motor. Unlike a robotaxi, they use airspace and don’t get stuck in traffic, they are confined to its track network, have specific parking/staging areas, use electric motors with track power, and use small stations. While Swyft cabins travel on fixed cables (similar to a gondola or the RopeTaxi but those are propelled by the cable), Ottobahn cabins travel on regular tracks at 37mph. For longer distances Ottobahn claims up to 150mph. Both use track switches to guide cabins to their destination.

Ottobahn cabins hang off a bogie which is powered by an electric motor with regular wheels and steel tracks. Cabins either stop at elevated stations or can employ a lift mechanism which drops the cabin to the sidewalk for on- and off-boarding. Ottobahn claims they can support 6000 riders per hour in each direction, or even more with a favorable network design. Similar to a monorail, their track is supported by towers about 120ft apart and between 15 and 30ft high. The track can also cross longer distances over rivers and other obstacles akin to a suspension bridge. Cabins can usually climb up to 7%, with extra support even 12%. That may allow a ship canal crossing.
Swyft is hoping to start projects in Queenstown, Miami, or Los Angeles. Ottobahn started construction of its first network in Phuket .

Traditional train lines serve stations along a linear corridor. Turning a train around at the end of the line takes time as the operator usually has to switch from one end of the train to the other. Lines may branch towards the outer area of a network, but that splits the headway on each branch. As automated train systems do not need to worry about a driver, they can switch direction more easily and offer a bit more flexibility. For example, they can serve short stub lines by backing in and out, though that may impact travel time. PRT systems are not bound to any fixed line/schedule, can use a more elaborate track network, branch on demand, skip stations, and only stop as necessary. Though each cabin may be smaller, short headways may still allow for sufficient capacity.

Any of these systems promise simpler/faster guideway and station construction, easier integration into the existing urban infrastructure, more flexible branching capabilities, and more convenience for riders. It may be worthwhile to consider them for West Seattle or Ballard and other future lines.

articles.title: Seattle Street Ends: Eastlake
articles.author: John Feit (Guest Contributor)
paras: Today we will visit eight street ends and one park in the Eastlake neighborhood. In previous posts, we have looked at street ends around West Seattle , South Ship Canal , from Ballard to Fremont , from Fremont to Portage Bay , as well as the Duwamish Waterway . The last post was for South Lake Union's street ends .

For those new to this series, a little background on Seattle’s Shoreline Street Ends is helpful. Because Seattle is bounded and divided by numerous fresh and salt bodies of water the city has what are called ‘street ends’ — streets that end when they encounter a water body often continue under the water, sometimes resulting in mini-parks or recreational spaces. There are hundreds of such occurrences – almost as many as there are east-west and north-south streets.
Many of them, 142 to be exact, are part of a Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) program called Shoreline Street Ends. The program’s goals are to:

A little over half of the 142 street ends are defined by SDOT as “worth a visit,” while the remainder are either “not yet ready for visitors” or have “no public access.” Street ends are concentrated along the Ship Canal and Lake Washington, but also occur along each of the city’s other shorelines. Working with the city and neighborhoods to secure funding, pass legislation, and organize work parties, the non-profit and all-volunteer Friends of Street Ends help ensure Seattle’s accessible street ends grow in number and those already serving visitors continue to thrive.

Shoreline Street Ends vary in character from sandy beaches to docks wedged amongst shipyards and industrial uses. They are spacious and they are compact, and most are very easy to find. They support habitat for native species of flora and fauna and are convenient places to launch a kayak, sailboat, or motorboat. Oftentimes, they are adjacent to waterfront parks, expanding upon those assets. They are as varied as Seattle’s topography, and you can visit them any time.
Cycling is the best way to visit Seattle’s shoreline street ends. Many are accessed from low-traffic streets or bike paths.

Sitting beneath the Interstate 5 Ship Canal Bridge is the Furman Street street end. A fairly simple affair, it has a broad grass lawn leading to the water and a view towards the University of Washington campus and the several new highrises emerging in its neighborhood. Along Fuhrman and next to the street end is a rowing club, adding a nice buzz of activity.

WSDOT has closed the area off between the rowing club and the street end due to some hazards associated with falling debris from the underside of the bridge while it undergoes repairs. This condition will remain for some time until all necessary repairs are made. That being said it’s still worth a peek.

Partly sandy beach and partly forested landscape, the Martin Street street end can appear mysterious when viewed from Fairview Avenue due to its dense tree canopy and deep shadows. Probing beyond the shadows, however, one can find a waterfront bathed in sunlight. When I visited I happened upon a festive gathering that expanded my appreciation of street ends to be about more than water access and places to catch a view of the water to include unique social and gathering places. Residents from recent apartment development in the neighborhood have added new energy to what used to be a more isolated street end.
SDOT recently finished $375,000 in improvements (most done after these photos were taken). Even if you’ve previously visited the street end, here is a good reason to go again.

The most improved of Eastlake’s street ends, and among the most improved of those I have visited, is the East Allison Street street end. Although lacking the shelter and intimacy of East Martin Street, its staging area for watercraft, generous steps leading to the shoreline, and ADA accessible parking, make it very user friendly.
Right across from the street end is a new neighborhood corner coffee shop, adding a nice amenity to an otherwise desirable location.

East Hamlin Street combines many of the endearing features of Seattle’s street ends, albeit in rustic packaging. It provides a fantastic prospect for viewing Gas Works Park and an intimate lagoon with a sandy shoreline. Other amenities include park benches, a picnic table, as well as an ever changing assortment of lawn chairs along the waterline. The plantings include rose bushes, seagrasses, and a variety of other flora I’m ill equipped to identify. I especially liked the large deciduous trees hovering along its northern edge, their hues changing to golden in the fall day’s crisp air.

Things have been a little tidied up since I took these photos. The paths have new gravel and the benches were repaired, and the neighborhood stewards have done a great job improving and keeping the plantings looking great.

South of East Hamlin Street is East Edgar Street. Although not (yet) part of the Street End program, the Seattle Parks Foundation has information on potential improvements that you can learn more about.

Situated at the tail end of one of Eastlake’s few east-west arterials, Roanoke Street can be hard to miss despite its strategic location and generous amenities. If one looks beyond the parking area along its eastern edge, one finds new street furniture and a paved plaza.

Just to the north is a densely packed, and very urban collection of houseboats. Unlike other neighboring houseboat communities, those along Mallard Cove are arranged parallel to the shoreline giving them a density different from neighboring houseboat communities. This effect is further enhanced by the hillside buildings’ eastern edge.
Boeing’s first factory was located at the foot of Roanoke street.

Unique among the dozens of street ends I visited in the past, Louisa Street has a bocce court and a color theme, whose red brilliance was enhanced by the crimson trees hovering above its like-colored furniture when I visited in the fall.

Neighbors are calling it the Louisa Street Beach since children are having fun playing games in the sand. The two trees to the north have mulch and edging to keep users off the tree roots and we will do additional planting this Fall. This park gets lots of kayak use - a self-service rental is across the street. It also generally has someone simply sitting there and enjoying the day—in all kinds of weather.

Lynn Street Mini Park has a range of amenities and terrific views. Its sandy shoreline is a favorite launching spot for kayakers, and its generously furnished street level terrace allows one to glance above the water enthusiasts to Lake Union. Framed by houseboats to the south and a rare over the water condominium to the north, the park provides one of the more unique and beloved edges along the lake. Although not part of SDOT’s Street End program, and officially a Seattle City Park, its designation matters not for appreciating its fine qualities.

The East Boston Street street end is easily missed unless one has a map in hand. The street end itself is really just the sidewalk along Fairview Avenue – there is no access to the water. Instead, and if one picks just the right viewing angle to snatch a view between the heavily vegetated shoreline one is surprised to see a picturesque assembly of houseboats framing a view across the lake to Queen Anne.

East Newton Street, also known as Terry Pettus Park , is currently undergoing renovation. Prior to its being closed I was able to visit it on a fine fall day in 2023. This particular street end, at least prior to its renovation, had that rarest of amenities: a dock. The dock not only allows one a different way to access the water but it also provides a view back to the shoreline.

It is hard to pick a favorite among the many great street ends along Eastlake Avenue, but Newton Street would certainly be a contender. All construction permits for the renovation have been obtained and I’m sure the neighborhood eagerly awaits its reopening. Click here for project updates.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Cascadia High-Speed Rail and I-5
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: To plan the next generation of north-south travel in western Washington, the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) is working on the I-5 Master Plan and the Cascadia High Speed Rail project. These two projects have been integrated into a combined Cascaida Program . WSDOT is asking for your feedback on what should be prioritized as the program progresses. The survey closes tonight so be sure to fill it out today.

The Cascadia Program is focused on the transportation of people and goods between Portland, Seattle, and Vancouver (BC). While this corridor crosses two states and an international boarder, 88% of the route is located in Washington. As a result, WSDOT is leading the effort while working with agencies in Oregon and British Columbia.

The survey asks about how and why you travel throughout the megaregion today as well as your priorities for I-5 and HSR. For I-5, WSDOT is in the process of identifying potential solutions to congestion, aging infrastructure, freight mobility, and connections to communities and other transportation modes. WSDOT expects to publish the I-5 Master Plan in 2028. Implementation of the recommended projects will start in the following years.

The other half of the Cascadia Program, high-speed rail, is still in the early stages of development. HSR would use trains that travel up to 160 mph/260 kph, more than double the current top speed of Amtrak Cascades. WSDOT has confirmed that a HSR route would not replace Amtrak Cascades. The WSDOT team is working on a Service Development Plan that will outline potential route options, explore operational components such as the number of stops and service frequency, and identify potential governance and funding options. articles.title: Shoreline Pedestrian Bridge Defect Jeopardizes Already Delayed Timeline
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Any remaining hope of Shoreline opening its new pedestrian bridge over I-5 this winter appear dashed, after the project ran into a snag this month. KIRO reporter Chris Sullivan broke the news on Tuesday, noting builders were delaying the bridge placement that had been slated for November.

“Unfortunately, the contractor has discovered some manufacturing issues with one of the arches,” a City spokesperson told KIRO . “They are currently working with the manufacturer to resolve the issue. At this point, it is unclear if the manufacturer will be able to make corrections on site with the existing arch or if they will have to make a whole new arch. It will be another couple of weeks before they know for sure, and we have a new timeline.”

While Shoreline and its contractor, Kraemer North America, are still determining the extent of the issue, the City is framing it as a minor setback, with a spring 2027 opening still feasible. In fact, the City's project website portrays a spring 2027 opening as essentially the plan all along.

However, that would represent a significant delay from initial plans. In 2020, The Urbanist reported Shoreline was still hoping to open the pedestrian bridge close to concurrently with the light rail station. Lining up funding added planning delays, but an early 2026 opening had still been targeted once the project's $40 million budget had been assembled in 2024 , as Urbanist coverage noted at the time.

"While the project was in design we developed an early 2026 opening estimate. Securing final approvals to advertise for construction bids took longer than we anticipated, delaying that step by several months," Shoreline spokesperson Tavia Tan told The Urbanis t. "We advertised for bids in December 2024. Once the contractor joined the project, we updated the schedule based on the bridge manufacturer’s production timeline and input from the construction team. Those factors led to an estimate of 'early 2027' for the full bridge opening. Earlier this fall, we revised that projection to spring of 2027, primarily due to delays in procuring materials. This revision occurred before we identified the manufacturing issue."

Shoreline's two light rail stations opened on August 30, 2024, along with the rest of the Lynnwood Link extension . While the City had hoped to open the bridge as close to possible as light rail's arrival, it could end up being close to three years after the fact.

Once the pedestrian bridge is in place, residents in the rapidly densifying neighborhood to the west of I-5, which Shoreline rezoned in 2016 , will have direct access to South Shoreline Station without having to head down to the busy overpass at 145th Street – a street that is being supercharged with highway-style roundabouts.

If plans to place the bridge span this month had gone forward, the project still had other hurdles to clear before it could have opened, including completing a direct ramp to the light rail station platform and a trail connection on the west side linking people walking, rolling, and biking to 1st Avenue NE, a corridor which has been among the focal points of midrise development in the area.
The contractor plans to move forward with the trail work while the bridge span issue is being rectified.

"The original construction schedule called for placing the bridge span before building the connecting trail to 1st Avenue NE," Tan said. "The contractor has rearranged the work and is now building the trail. This flexibility allows construction to continue and helps limit delays while we determine the next steps for the bridge."

Sullivan noted a brief night-time freeway closure will be necessary once the bridge span is ready for installation: "You have likely seen the massive structure being built along the west side of the freeway for months. Shoreline had targeted Saturday, Nov. 7, or Saturday, Nov. 14, as the nights to close I-5 and lift the bridge into place. That installation has been delayed, but other work on the project is continuing."

Despite the lack of a pedestrian bridge, both of Shoreline's stations have been success stories, generating robust homebuilding activity and solid initial ridership numbers . Shoreline South averaged more than 3,600 daily boardings in October, boosted by a bus restructure that truncated Sound Transit's Route 522 bus at the station.

Shoreline North hovered around 2,800 daily boardings in September and October. Overall, the 1 Line corridor amassed just over 155,000 daily boardings in October, making it the busiest light rail system in the United States.
The addition of Shoreline's pedestrian bridge and continued residential growth offer a potent combination to build on that momentum.

articles.title: Five More Washington Cities Selected for State Growth Plan Reviews in 2027
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Washington's Commerce Department has released a list of five cities and towns that will see their housing growth plans subjected to additional state scrutiny next year, the second set of reviews planned under the 2025 Housing Accountability Act . Burlington, Friday Harbor, Mount Vernon, Oak Harbor, and Washougal will go under the microscope, with city leaders given deadlines to make any updates to their local Comprehensive Plans with the goal of ensuring that development regulations intended to pave the way for more diverse housing types across a range of income levels are in place.

The 2027 cities are mostly clustered around the north end of Puget Sound, in counties that had a state-mandated December 31, 2025 deadline to overhaul their local Comprehensive Plans. All five cities faced that deadline and didn't meet it, either leaving Commerce out of the loop when it comes to updating their plan or submitting a draft plan that the state found to fall short in some way.

The Housing Accountability Act represents something of a sea change in local housing growth planning that cities are still getting used to. Prior to its implementation, the only way to challenge a Comprehensive Plan that looked to be out-of-compliance with state law was to file a challenge at the state's Growth Management Hearings Board, a case-by-case appeal process that usually fell on private groups like neighborhood organizations or the statewide land use advocacy non-profit Futurewise to pursue.

Though the Commerce Department is often tasked with providing recommendations on local development standards and zoning changes, there wasn't a mechanism available to hold cities and towns that went too far their own way accountable. With the Housing Accountability Act, cities and towns are given a compliance deadline to make essential changes and if those aren't enacted, the so-called Builder's Remedy goes into effect – with local permit departments unable to deny building permits for residential projects that meet certain affordability requirements, regardless of the underlying zoning. Theoretically, that could mean skyscrapers in areas of the city that aren't used to dense housing.

Commerce is still in the middle of its 2026 "selected review" process, with zoning changes already adopted in three of the eight jurisdictions that made the list this year. So far, only Carnation has gotten to the stage of approving a final plan that is still being reviewed by Commerce, with Bainbridge Island and the 300-resident town of Beaux Arts Village both adopting interim regulations that provide additional time to adopt permanent changes down the road.

Next week, the City of DuPont, tucked into South Pierce County near Joint Base Lewis-McChord, is poised to be the first city to actually trigger the Builder's Remedy. Despite a timeline that doesn't call for adoption of potential changes to the city's Comprehensive Plan until early next year, DuPont has not requested an extension from Commerce that would prevent the Builder's Remedy from taking effect.

Though many of the jurisdictions that have been subjected to review so far have been relatively small, the impact is adding up. By the end of the second year, Commerce is on track to have reviewed cities and towns accounting for approximately 144,000 residents, more people than live in Washington's sixth largest city of Kent.

In turning its attention to Friday Harbor, Commerce will be jumping into the fray when it comes to one of the state's thorniest housing crises. As a tourist-oriented city with a high rate of seasonal housing, housing in Friday Harbor is regularly out-of-reach of the workers that the local economy relies on. Housing prices within San Juan County rose more than 100% between 2016 and 2022, far faster than median wages could ever compete with.

Despite increased demand for units in Friday Harbor, projects proposed in the city often turn highly contentious. Last year, a 49-unit development near Friday Harbor elementary school drew significant opposition, despite the inclusion of eight units of workforce housing in the project. The concerns raised included increased traffic, traffic safety impacts, and a lack of overall infrastructure, but the common denominator was the idea that Friday Harbor can't handle more population density.

Amanda Lynn, Executive Director of the San Juan Community Home Trust, offered an overall view of housing growth on San Juan Island, in an interview with the The Journal of the San Juans about that specific project.

“Every time you add a housing unit on this island, that requires infrastructure, that requires community resources like fire, police, school, anything you can think of,” Lynn said. “Every housing unit requires these things. So there’s always a balance beyond even just thinking about the ecosystem balance of the island itself.”
That balancing act, while clearly necessary in some regard on a ferry-dependent island, often means that lower-income residents trying to find homes in San Juan Island get the short end of the stick.

A state review under the Housing Accountability Act won't be able to fully solve Friday Harbor's housing crisis, of course. But it will likely ensure that barriers that stand in the way of housing production that aren't aligned with state law don't stay in place, adding clear repercussions if they do.

As these reviews continue to ramp up, pushback from local elected officials is another thing to watch for. As Beaux Arts Village councilmembers took their vote on interim development regulations last month, they also vowed to push for legislative changes that would modify the Housing Accountability Act to be less impactful on them. So far, what exactly it would look like to water down the legislation hasn't become clear, but as larger cities start to get subjected to that review, the political pressure could ramp up.

For now, however, the Housing Accountability Act does appear to be having its intended impact, slowly bringing along jurisdictions that otherwise would be lagging when it comes to legalizing housing, one by one.

articles.title: The Stranger’s Noise Complaint: XOË
articles.author: Stranger Staff
paras: Welcome to Noise Complaint, The Stranger ‘s new audio and video music podcast featuring live performances right here at The Stranger HQ. Streamed live and released every other Friday, we invite a great band, musician, or wonderfully weird act to perform. Tune in, discover something new, and support art in your city.

The output of XOË—Zoë Duarte (vocals), Max Irvine (keyboards, guitar), Saba Samakar (drums), Adrian Michael (bass, guitar, drums)—is small so far, but it instantly ensnares you in its charms. Capturing a big chunk of your attention is the slyly seductive grain of Duarte’s voice, which, incidentally, is summarized by the title of their fantastic song “Sweet Sensation.” XOË (pronounced “X-O-E”) really blossom on their most recent release, the stellar Blur of a Dream EP; the slow-motion whirlpool of “Feed Me” is as dankly alluring as early Tricky. The earlier track “Nighttime Blues” bears the erotic mesmerism as Scritti Politti’s “The ’Sweetest Girl.’” Boudoir-friendly R&B may be the band’s dominant mode, but Irvine’s capable of florid keyboard arabesques worthy of jazz legends George Duke and Chick Corea. XOË even have a savvy interpretation of Nick Drake’s dream-folk classic “Pink Moon” in their arsenal. It’s certain that they have even more wonderful surprises for us on the horizon. DAVE SEGAL

articles.title: Maintenance of automated trains
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: Sound Transit has recently reduced construction cost with smaller station designs (for example Alaska Junction) but their current four-car trains are 380ft long while Vancouver’s SkyTrains are only 280ft long. That still requires bigger, harder to locate, and more expensive stations. Due to automation SkyTrain can operate more frequently and therefore still handle higher ridership while providing higher convenience. Sound Transit has considered automation but is concerned about interoperability with current trains. They could add an operator on surface portions such as through Rainier Valley. If they would keep the Ballard line separate, then interoperability would not be an issue, but Sound Transit would need to worry about where to park them at night (“stabling”), clean them, and maintain them. When Sound Transit considered a starter line for Ballard, they concluded that they would need to build an operations and maintenance facility (OMF) in Interbay and that its cost would offset all savings. I gathered some ideas on how to potentially reduce such effort.

If you connect the Ballard (starter) line with the main line, you could still use the existing Central OMF in SODO. If such a connection is not feasible, then you could build a separate regular OMF or consider other options.

For maintenance, you could connect to the BNSF tracks at Interbay and SODO to move trains between the Ballard line and the SODO OMF during off-hours. As BNSF tracks are not electrified, you would need a separate locomotive to pull the trains. You could also truck the trains as these occasional maintenance events.
For nightly cleaning and monthly maintenance, you may still want a separate small cleaning center just like SeaTac airport cleans their people movers locally.

When Lynnwood Link opened, Sound Transit did not have enough stabling space at the Central OMF. They parked some trains at various stations at night . Operators had to pick them up there in the morning and park them there at night. Automated trains may operate through the night. If you do not want to operate through the night to maintain the tracks, you can park automated trains anywhere. They can wake themselves up in the morning, go through safety checks, and move to the first station by themselves. In fact, if Sound Transit wants to reduce service in the evening and start cleaning cars, they could send them to the OMF for daily cleaning and afterwards park them at any pocket track. If they want to reduce service further, they even reduce service to a single track towards the end of the line and use the other track for stabling.
This would reduce the size and cost of the OMF considerably. As automated trains can move (“shunting”) themselves in and out of the OMF, there is no need for shunting staff.
Sound Transit could even allow construction of transit-oriented housing above such facility as the Hong Kong MTA has done for example.
If Ballard trains don’t need to use the Central OMF in SODO, Sound Transit may be able to reduce the size of the Everett OMF. This may shift some of the cost.

I would hope by reducing the cost of the maintenance facility, Sound Transit would consider an automated Ballard starter line and shorter stations. Due to its lower cost, it could connect Ballard sooner and also be more attractive to riders due to its higher frequency and longer service hours.
